analysis.one_liner: Lets cities and towns build their own broadband even when their state bans it.
analysis.headline: The Community Broadband Act of 2018 died in committee without ever getting a vote, after being referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in January 2018.
analysis.plain_summary: Many states have laws that stop cities, counties, and towns from building their own high-speed internet networks, usually where an existing cable or phone company already provides service. This bill would amend federal telecom law to say no state can prohibit a local government, state agency, or Indian tribe from offering broadband, while requiring that a government-run network not favor itself when it regulates private competitors. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of towns, cities, and tribal areas — especially in states that currently ban or restrict municipal broadband — who could get publicly built high-speed internet as an alternative to the local cable or phone company. Rural and underserved communities where private providers have not built fast networks stand to gain the most. City and county governments gain the power to decide for themselves whether to build a network.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents in states banning city-owned internet

how_it_helps.text: Overrides state laws that prohibit local governments from offering broadband, restoring the ability of a city, county, state agency, or Indian tribe to act as a public provider of advanced telecommunications capability.
Covers 'any service that utilizes' broadband, so a public provider could offer the actual retail internet service residents buy, not just underlying infrastructure.
Bars a government-run network from discriminating in favor of itself when it regulates competing private providers, addressing the main fairness objection to municipal competition.
Keeps public providers subject to the same federal and state telecom rules that apply to every other provider, so they compete on the same legal footing rather than an exempted one.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable, phone, and wireless companies would face new competition from government-owned networks in their service areas, including in markets they have had to themselves under state bans. State legislatures would lose authority to block local broadband projects. If a municipal network is poorly run, local taxpayers could be on the hook for its costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable and telecom incumbents, some states

drawbacks.text: A municipal network built into low demand or mismanaged can leave local taxpayers covering the losses, which is why opponents favor local voter approval over a federal override of state rules.

The bill removes state oversight entirely — it forbids any state law that has the 'effect of prohibiting' public broadband — so states could not require feasibility studies, referendums, or financing checks before a city builds a network.

Critics argue that government-owned networks compete unfairly with private companies on taxes, financing, and regulatory treatment; the bill addresses discrimination in rulemaking but leaves those structural advantages in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans in places where the local cable or phone company is the only option, a competing public network can mean lower prices, better service, and coverage where private companies declined to build. The main honest cost is execution risk: broadband networks are expensive, and a badly run municipal one falls on local taxpayers, which is the strongest case for the state guardrails this bill would sweep away. The bill tries to blunt the fairness objection by barring a public provider from favoring itself in regulation and keeping it subject to the same telecom rules as private firms, but it deliberately takes the decision away from state legislatures that have chosen to restrict municipal networks.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee in January 2018, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Anna Eshoo and six other House Democrats introduced the Community Broadband Act on January 17, 2018.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over telecommunications.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

The bill would have amended Section 706 of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to bar states from prohibiting public providers — states, political subdivisions, their agencies, or Indian tribes — from offering advanced telecommunications capability.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone companies are better off, because state laws keeping municipal networks off the market stayed in place and they kept their service areas uncontested. State legislatures that had restricted city-run broadband also kept that authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable and telecom incumbents kept their markets

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Broadband Act on January 17, 2018.

for.name: Reps. Michael Doyle, Keith Ellison, Ro Khanna, Beto O'Rourke, Mark Pocan, and Jared Polis
for.role: Original cosponsors who joined the introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications and Technology Subcommittee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Incumbent broadband and cable companies
against.role: Largest providers of home internet service
against.what_they_did: The broadband industry has long pushed state legislatures to restrict municipal broadband networks, and such state restrictions are exactly what this bill would have overridden; no industry group supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — Eshoo plus six original cosponsors and two more for eight total — and no Republican signed on; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican, so the Democratic side showed support and the Republican-controlled committee showed none.

industries.note: State laws banning or restricting municipal networks have protected incumbent cable and phone companies from public competition in their service areas; this bill would have removed that protection nationwide, letting a city build a rival network wherever residents wanted one. Companies that profit from being the only local option lose pricing power and customers.

industries.industry: State governments that restrict municipal broadband
industries.note: The bill strips states of the power to prohibit local broadband projects, overriding laws roughly twenty states have passed limiting or banning city-run networks. Local governments and their residents gain the decision instead.

industries.industry: Indian tribes with unmet connectivity needs
industries.note: Tribal governments are explicitly named as eligible public providers, giving tribes a federal-law route to build networks on their land even if a state's rules would otherwise block them.
